main.title: Panzer Dragoon Orta
main.summary: Panzer Dragoon Orta is a 2002 rail shooter game developed by Smilebit and published by Sega for the Xbox.

cards.text: Panzer Dragoon Orta is a 2002 rail shooter game developed by Smilebit and published by Sega for the Xbox. The fourth Panzer Dragoon game, it was released in Japan in 2002 and in North America and Europe in 2003. The story follows a girl, Orta, who is freed by a dragon and embarks on a quest to prevent the abuse of ancient technology. The gameplay features the player moving an aiming reticle and shooting enemies while the dragon flies through 3D environments on a predetermined track.

Production of Orta began in 2001. The previous Panzer Dragoon development team, Team Andromeda, had disbanded after the release of Panzer Dragoon Saga (1998). Around a dozen staff returned to work on Orta, including the artists Takashi Iwade and Kentaro Yoshida, the composer Saori Kobayashi and the battle designer Akihiko Mukaiyama, who directed Orta. While the greater power of the Xbox allowed for more freedom in gameplay and graphical design, the production was troubled by a lack of art design direction and problems with the team's graphical and gameplay ambitions.

Panzer Dragoon Orta received critical acclaim, with praise for its gameplay and art design. Several publications have named it one of the best Xbox games, and it is remembered favorably for its gameplay and technical achievements. Panzer Dragoon staff have voiced mixed feelings regarding Orta for its continuation of the story after Saga. Orta was the final Panzer Dragoon game until the 2020 remake of the original Panzer Dragoon.

main.title: EyeToy camera
main.subtitle: Your movements become the controls
main.summary: EyeToy brought camera-based play to PlayStation 2 in 2003.

cards.heading: A camera in the living room
cards.text: EyeToy is a USB camera for PlayStation 2. Introduced in 2003, it put the player's image on the television and let specially designed games respond to movement in front of the camera. The person playing became part of the picture rather than controlling everything with a handheld pad.

cards.heading: Games built around movement
cards.text: EyeToy: Play built short activities around this idea. The camera required compatible software designed to use its input. Other titles, including games in The Sims and Tony Hawk series, added optional EyeToy features.

main.title: Steam
main.subtitle: The library becomes a service
main.summary: Valve's platform helped reshape how PC games are distributed, updated and kept together.

cards.heading: The library becomes an account
cards.text: Steam began in 2003 and developed from a way of delivering updates into a large PC storefront and social platform. A game library increasingly became an account linked to downloads, automatic updates and online features.

cards.heading: Preserving software that keeps changing
cards.text: Convenience also changed the responsibilities of preservation. Installers, dependencies and particular versions can matter as much as a boxed disc. A service-based library raises new questions about continuity when software and infrastructure keep changing.

features.title: What sits behind a library
features.summary: An account changes how a collection works.

cards.heading: Remember a service by its games
cards.text: Valve announced the Steam client's release on 12 September 2003. Twenty years later, its anniversary page arranged the service's history around each year's leading releases, mixing games with illustrations and memories of popular culture. That was one way to make an expanding service understandable: start with the titles people encountered there. Yet a library view tells only part of the story. Behind the remembered games are accounts, software and rules of access. Following those less visible parts shows how a collection can depend on a continuing relationship with a platform.

cards.heading: A familiar word, a specific licence
cards.text: The Steam Subscriber Agreement describes access to software as a licence. In the version consulted in 2026, buying content does not transfer ownership of its intellectual property, and an account or subscription cannot simply be transferred except where Valve permits it. The everyday idea of a personal collection therefore sits inside a specific agreement. These are the terms of the version consulted in 2026. The relevant questions are which account has access and what that access includes.

cards.heading: The client becomes part of starting
cards.text: Valve's developer documentation explains another connection between a game and its platform. The Steam DRM wrapper checks ownership and starts Steam before starting the game so that Steamworks features can function. Developers can choose whether to use this integration tool. For a developer, launching a game can involve services outside its own executable. For a player, those steps may appear as one ordinary click. The documentation makes that small sequence legible, showing some of the software relationships hidden behind the library's Play button.

cards.heading: Sharing is also a designed system
cards.text: Steam Families, released in 2024, made eligible games accessible across a family group while keeping personal saves and achievements. Multiple copies determined how many people could play the same title together. Developers could also exclude games, and technical requirements could limit sharing. These details show why a shared library is more than a row of borrowed covers. It has to organise separate people, available copies and progress. The result offers a particular kind of household access, shaped by software and participation rules rather than by passing a physical disc between hands.

main.title: Puyo Pop Fever
main.summary: Puyo Pop Fever is a 2003 puzzle video game developed by Sonic Team and published by Sega.

cards.text: Puyo Pop Fever is a 2003 puzzle video game developed by Sonic Team and published by Sega. It is the fifth main installment in the Puyo Puyo series, and the second Puyo Puyo game to be programmed by Sonic Team after Puyo Pop (which was released just after the series' original developer, Compile, went bankrupt). This was the start of what can be considered a reboot of the Puyo Puyo franchise, with this entry's plot revolving around Professor Accord losing her flying cane.

Sega, which acquired the series' character rights from Compile in 1998, and eventually the full rights in 2001, published all the Japanese releases of the game, and also published the arcade and GameCube versions internationally. The game was scarcely released internationally, and certain versions were released by other publishers in those areas.

main.title: Project Gotham Racing 2
main.summary: Project Gotham Racing 2 is a 2003 arcade-style racing video game developed by Bizarre Creations and published by Microsoft Game Studios.

cards.heading: Project Gotham Racing 2
cards.text: Project Gotham Racing 2 is a 2003 arcade-style racing video game developed by Bizarre Creations and published by Microsoft Game Studios. It was released exclusively for the Xbox in 2003 as the successor to 2001's Project Gotham Racing.

cards.heading: More cities and ways to earn Kudos
cards.text: Development began shortly after the completion of the first game and was first made official in August 2002. Bill Gates himself had emailed suggestions to the developer team of what he wished to see in it. The Kudos system, challenges set, available cars, and the tracks around which players race were expanded greatly from the original. The Kudos system was made to be slightly more forgiving than before and expanded to include new moves like drafting a rival or performing a 360. Alongside the 10 new real-world cities (and the Nürburgring) track, two additional packs were released as DLC.

cards.heading: A celebrated Xbox racer
cards.text: Project Gotham Racing 2 was critically acclaimed and is often considered one of the Xbox's greatest exclusive titles. It was followed up by Project Gotham Racing 3 in 2005.

main.title: Devil May Cry 2
main.summary: Devil May Cry 2 is a 2003 action-adventure game developed and published by Capcom for the PlayStation 2.

cards.heading: Devil May Cry 2
cards.text: Devil May Cry 2 is a 2003 action-adventure game developed and published by Capcom for the PlayStation 2. In terms of chronological order, the game's events are set after Devil May Cry and Devil May Cry: The Animated Series and prior to Devil May Cry 4.

cards.heading: Dante and Lucia face Arius
cards.text: Set in modern times, in the fictional Vie de Marli island, the story centers on demon hunter Dante and island guardian Lucia in their fight to stop a businessman named Arius from raising the demon Argosax and achieving supreme power. The story is told primarily through a mixture of cutscenes using the game engine, with several pre-rendered full motion videos.

cards.heading: A troubled production divides the audience
cards.text: Handled by a different team that lacked experience, Devil May Cry 2 had a troubled production which was reflected in its reception. The game received mixed reviews and has been criticized for a variety of decisions, which made it considerably different from its predecessor; chief among these were the lowered difficulty and changes to Dante's personality. Despite that, Devil May Cry 2 was a commercial success, established a number of series conventions, and motivated its development team to improve their work, staying with the franchise for future entries.

main.title: Lifeline
main.summary: Lifeline, released in Japan as Operator's Side, is a 2003 survival horror adventure video game developed and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2.

cards.text: Lifeline, released in Japan as Operator's Side, is a 2003 survival horror adventure video game developed and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2. Set in the near future aboard a space hotel attacked by unidentified monsters, the game follows the player as they direct cocktail waitress Rio Hohenheim to safety while searching for the player's girlfriend Naomi as well as the source of the monster infestation.

Lifeline's defining aspect is its voice user interface: the vast majority of gameplay is conducted by using the PlayStation 2's microphone to issue commands, which are interpreted by the game via speech recognition to control Rio and dictate her movements and actions.

Lifeline was released on January 30, 2003, in Japan and March 2, 2004, in North America by Konami; in Japan, it was optionally sold alongside the PlayStation 2 headset. It received generally mixed reviews, with praise for its innovation and potential but criticism for the low reliability of its speech recognition. However, Lifeline still sold well enough to be rereleased in Japan on September 25, 2003, under Sony's The Best budget range, and the game has maintained somewhat of a cult following over the years since its release for its innovative gameplay and the depth of its voice mechanics.

main.title: Disgaea: Hour of Darkness
main.summary: Disgaea: Hour of Darkness is a tactical role-playing video game developed and published by Nippon Ichi Software for the PlayStation 2.

cards.text: Disgaea: Hour of Darkness is a tactical role-playing video game developed and published by Nippon Ichi Software for the PlayStation 2. Set in a world full of demons and angels, the story follows Laharl, the son of a demon overlord, who upon being awakened after a two-year slumber, aspires to succeed his father's place while also fighting rival demons in the process.

Nippon Ichi has also licensed or produced a wide variety of Disgaea merchandise, including a manga. In 2006, Nippon Ichi released a sequel called Disgaea 2: Cursed Memories for the PlayStation 2, as well as a 12-episode anime adaptation titled Makai Senki Disgaea. A PlayStation Portable version of Disgaea: Hour of Darkness was released entitled Disgaea: Afternoon of Darkness, as was a Windows port titled Disgaea PC. A HD remake, Disgaea 1 Complete, was released for Nintendo Switch and PlayStation 4 and later for iOS and Android.

In 2004, the game received a spiritual sequel, Phantom Brave. Disgaea D2: A Brighter Darkness was released for PlayStation 3 in 2013, and stars the main cast (and additional new characters) of Hour of Darkness.

main.title: Game Boy Advance SP
main.subtitle: A folding Game Boy Advance
main.summary: An upgraded Game Boy Advance with a folding case, rechargeable battery and integrated screen lighting.

cards.heading: Game Boy Advance SP
cards.text:
The Game Boy Advance SP (SP stands for "Special") is a handheld game console developed and marketed by Nintendo. The SP is an upgraded version of the Game Boy Advance with a more compact clamshell design.

The SP was the first Game Boy device with a rechargeable battery, and the first widely released model with an integrated screen light, starting with front lighting and later transitioning to backlighting. The light made it easier to play in low-light conditions than its predecessors, which relied on reflective screens. It was followed by the Game Boy Micro in 2005.

cards.heading: Satoru Okada and the folding prototype
cards.text: The Game Boy Advance SP was championed by Satoru Okada, who led the development of the original Game Boy Advance. When Okada first pitched to Nintendo leadership the idea of a small and thin Game Boy Advance that used a rechargeable battery, the feedback was almost entirely negative. Not deterred, Okada told one of his hardware engineers to build a conceptual model as small and thin as possible without regard to the feasibility of manufacturing the device. What resulted was the clamshell design of the Game Boy Advance SP. When Okada took this conceptual model to the same leadership group that rejected his initial pitch, they were quickly won over.

cards.heading: Illuminating the display
cards.text:
In addition to being smaller and using a rechargeable battery, the Game Boy Advance SP also addressed a key shortcoming of the original Game Boy Advance: the reflective color display that was hard to see in dark conditions.

The first Game Boy Advance SP had a frontlight that illuminated the front of the display and a reflective surface behind the screen that sent light back through the liquid crystal pixel elements to the viewer. A later revision replaced the frontlight and reflective surface with a backlight that also illuminated the liquid crystal pixel elements.

cards.heading: Headphones and the charging port
cards.text: Nintendo removed the 3.5 mm headphone jack from the SP, which had been included on all previous Game Boy models. Headphones designed specifically for the GBA SP can be purchased, or standard headphones can be attached with an optional adapter that plugs into the same port as the AC adapter. As both the AC adapter and headphones use the same port, it is not possible to charge the SP and listen to headphones at the same time with the Nintendo-brand adapter. There are, however, third-party adapters that "split" into two different cords: the power jack on one side and a headphone jack on the other.

main.title: Kung Fu Chaos
main.subtitle: A brawl takes place on a film set
main.summary: Kung Fu Chaos is Just Add Monsters' Xbox party fighting game, released in North America on 25 February 2003. Its stages are scenes in an imaginary martial-arts film, with a director commenting on the action as the cast attempts to survive it. Up to four players fight through sets that can be as important as the opponents occupying them. The film premise gives the game permission to change circumstances rapidly, replacing a stable arena with moving scenery, timed dangers and comic interruptions that demand attention beyond the person immediately being punched.

cards.heading: A brawl takes place on a film set
cards.text: Kung Fu Chaos is Just Add Monsters' Xbox party fighting game, released in North America on 25 February 2003. Its stages are scenes in an imaginary martial-arts film, with a director commenting on the action as the cast attempts to survive it. Up to four players fight through sets that can be as important as the opponents occupying them. The film premise gives the game permission to change circumstances rapidly, replacing a stable arena with moving scenery, timed dangers and comic interruptions that demand attention beyond the person immediately being punched.

cards.heading: A successful taunt is also a risk
cards.text: Quick and heavy attacks, throws, blocks and counters provide the basic fighting vocabulary. After defeating an enemy, a player can taunt to build towards a powerful special attack. Performing the taunt leaves the character briefly vulnerable, creating an opportunity for someone else to interrupt or steal the moment. The reward therefore depends on choosing when the scene is safe enough to celebrate. Campaign progress also requires a sufficient performance rating, connecting survival and fighting to the director's evaluation of the scene rather than merely reaching its final few seconds.

cards.heading: The first production of the future Ninja Theory
cards.text: Just Add Monsters began with a small, self-funded prototype before obtaining the support needed to finish the game. Reviews appreciated the tone and inventive stages while questioning the depth of the fighting; some also criticised its racial stereotypes. Sales disappointed, and a planned sequel was cancelled. The studio later became Ninja Theory and developed Heavenly Sword. Kung Fu Chaos established an early interest in strongly directed visual presentation, using the setting of a chaotic film shoot to make the level itself an active participant in the multiplayer brawl.
